utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. For urgent personal reasons, Judge Stole is unable to sit today. The remaining Judges of this Chamber are satisfied that it's in the interests of justice to continue sitting today. Judge Stole will be back at the first session after today's session. Mr. Krasniqi, may I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, you may continue your examination-in-chief. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examination by Mr. Di Fazio: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krasniqi. Mr. Krasniqi, I just want to ask you some questions about -- some personal questions about your son Pal Krasniqi. When he left to go to Jablanica, about that time was he a married or a single man?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was single.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if at the time he had a relationship with a Serb or Roma woman or had had in the past any relationship with a Serb or Roma girl?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know and I don't think he had any relation, any such relation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you some -- firstly, I'll put the question to you this way: Only answer the question if you're -- if you're sure about the answer, don't speculate, please. Do you know what he was wearing when you last saw him on the 10th of July, 1993 -- 1998?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: So he was wearing trainers, a T-shirt with stripes, and he had a collar which had a red stripe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What article precisely are trainers, what -- what did you mean by that? I just want to be sure about that.

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: White towards light blue trainers in colour.

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've used the expression "trainers," are you referring to shoes?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sport shoes, but not proper shoes, they're different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if your son possessed in July of 1998 any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm anticipating a leading question, so I'm rising before it occurs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether Mr. Di Fazio had it in mind. Mr. Guy-Smith, objection against a leading question is fine, of course, if there are very, very strong reasons to believe that someone is going to put a leading question. Anticipation is -- is not under all circumstances prohibited. But let's try not to be too -- to anticipate too much on what others are going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I wasn't planning on it but based on the language "Do you know if he had," considering the questions asked before, I was jumping to my feet. MR. DI FAZIO: [Microphone not activated] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I could imagine some 200 questions starting this way not being leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So can I, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- based on experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I'm sure there won't be any problem with this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that your son possessed trousers of some form or another in 1998?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I know. They -- they changed trousers and T-shirts and shirts among friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know -- I understand that. All I want to know is just a simple yes or no, I'm sure you can answer it very quickly. Simple yes or no, your son owned trousers, didn't he, in 19 -- July 1998?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know the village of Bardosan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, you leave it at this moment -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'm going to, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where it leaves a bit of a mystery. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I -- if Your Honours wish me to pursue the topic that I -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know exactly what the relevance is, it of course could be very relevant. I then asked myself to what extent that is so -- MR. DI FAZIO: I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- obvious that it might even be assumed without specific questions on the matter, and then of course the answer surprised me a bit. Well, ownership -- Mr. Krasniqi, did your son wear trousers usually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usually trousers, but at the time he was wearing some sports trousers, sports trainers he calls them. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What colour were they?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue with a white stripe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how old is he -- was he when he came and spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know his name exactly, but he was married and he was about 35 years old --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His age, interpreter's correction --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... should be a redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You spoke, Mr. Guy-Smith, when the witness was still speaking. I missed what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't know whether we should be in private session or perhaps there should be a redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am not -- MR. DI FAZIO: Can we go into private session very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Di Fazio, the Chamber, of course, received in addition to the statement also further information about the witness, and mention is made there of animosity between the witness, his son and Ukshini. Now, I could imagine that you consider this relevant information and that could shed, perhaps, some additional light on what happened; nevertheless, I didn't hear anything about it. Of course, it could be that you intentionally would leave it for cross-examination, but, of course, if the Chamber receives what - let me say in the abstract - could be a -- information about a circumstance that could, could, put a different light on what appears to be the gist of what -- of the evidence the Prosecution is presenting at this moment, of course, we are wondering whether that should be explored in one way or the other, so that you either exclude the animosity as -- as a possible explanation for events still not known in detail or whether -- or whether it should be taken as a possibility, a serious possibility, to explain things that happened. I'm just -- MR. DI FAZIO: I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I'm just wondering whether that needs some attention, yes or no, and whether you'd like to give that attention yourself or whether you are confident that attention will be given to it anyhow in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I would first like to -- yes, please -- I take it that you want -- perhaps not to respond for Mr. Di Fazio but at least to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'd like to add something, Your Honour, which is -- which is just this: The Chamber has clearly read the witness statement from this witness and I would refer the Chamber to paragraph 18, which is where the evidence that this witness has just given relates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And the Chamber will also note that the evidence given by this witness is a great amplification on what was previously said in the statement and a great amplification on what this witness, to our understanding, has ever previously said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That, however -- yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And the concern I have is in relation to the proofing sessions or what happened during the proofing sessions, because the Chamber will note, and the Chamber has picked up, that there was a note recorded by the Prosecution which records the fact that this witness said that Hamez Ukshini, about which this witness has just given evidence, was an enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Now, we're simply not on notice as to what this witness may have said to the Prosecution. It sounds like there was some form of proofing session with this witness sufficient to at least raise the concern that there was evidence which ought to be recorded. And I raise that concern at this point because at the very end of this witness's evidence, we are faced with new evidence which we haven't had notice of before and of which there appears to be no detailed notice of what this witness may or may not have said during a proofing session which may or may not have taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To some extent, of course, it's speculation. It may have been a very short proofing session. Proofing sessions are not -- I would say I would certainly not expect the Defence to take the view that proofing sessions are obligatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I say just, for the sake of clarification and in order to ensure the position is as accurately recorded as possible, make it clear that although neither Mr. Troop nor Mr. Harvey on behalf of Mr. Brahimaj were present, myself and Mr. Guy-Smith have had a conversation with Mr. Di Fazio about the genesis of the note to which Your Honour has referred, and we have received an explanation from him as to how that note came about. I wasn't alive to the fact that Mr. Troop was going to raise this, but we have received an explanation from Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you willing to -- I do understand that the explanation is not such that you would immediately join Mr. Troop in his concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you be willing to -- I don't know whether you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Di Fazio can explain the position for himself. It's just I wouldn't want it to be thought that I sat there silently associating myself with the suggestion that I knew nothing about the circumstances in which this note came about, when I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I'm not at this moment interested that much on how exactly the proofing session went on. I expect that relevant information is given if anything new arises, during these proofing sessions. I find a note in which at least there is a new element, and my concern at this moment was that although that information is there and that looking at it, one would not exclude for the possibility that it could be relevant to understand the events in full, and nevertheless it has not been dealt with in any way during the examination. And of course the Chamber would like to understand the testimony and context as well as can be. Now, I would suggest that during the next break, Mr. Emmerson, you share with Mr. Troop, first of all, the explanation that was given. And if there's any issue remaining, then the Chamber would like to hear of it. Let's first -- Mr. Di Fazio, let's go back to the issue I raised; that is, information that seems to be relevant. Did you intentionally not touch upon it or would you expect Defence to do it? Then, of course I would be satisfied, but -- MR. DI FAZIO: It's more a case of not considering it of any great moment, but I'm happy to go into this and to clarify it through the witness as much as possible about this issue, so that it's all clear and everyone knows exactly what his evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it will be clear or not, but at least it's then been dealt with. MR. DI FAZIO: So that it's been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- let's -- MR. DI FAZIO: It's not a problem at all. I'm more than willing to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's not spend then too much time on it, and I'm not seeking lengthy explanation on the matter but I'm just trying to understand what the relevance of the information -- MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is going to be. MR. DI FAZIO: -- I can do that. That's absolutely no problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has put on his headphones again, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Di Fazio has one or more additional questions to you, Mr. Krasniqi. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I would like you to explain to the Trial Chamber what your relationship was with this gentleman named Ukshini, and I would like you to tell the Trial Chamber what your relationship was with this man in July of 1998 and what it is now. So let's start firstly with July 1998. Did you know him? How did you get on with him? How did you -- how did you consider him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Di Fazio has this in mind, but the note records an issue about the relationship between the witness's son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But -- MR. DI FAZIO: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Emmerson, this was really too early. I mean, you can introduce a relationship with your son by asking first -- so therefore, you should have left Mr. Di Fazio his line of question. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- MR. DI FAZIO: And I will deal with that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my first question is: In 1998, what was your relationship with Ukshini and what is it -- what is it now?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ever since Ukshini was a student, I knew him. With his father, Ukshin Besa, we -- we had a good relationship. We visit -- we exchanged visits on occasions and so we knew each other. When I heard that my son was involved in this and that (redacted) had something to do with it, I went to ask for him. And then I recounted to you the talk we had, but I didn't learn anything from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not entirely clear from that answer whether you enjoyed a good relationship with him in 1998. Can you tell us if -- if that was the case?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a very good relationship with his father because this person, this other person, was very young to stay with us adults when we met together in ceremony or social occasions, but his father, yes. He was young. So, as I said, I went to meet him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do I take it from that answer - correct me if I'm wrong, I'm certainly not trying to make suggestions - but I just want to know: Did you know his father better than you knew Hamez Ukshini? Is that what -- do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Ukshini -- what age was Ukshini in 1998? Was he about your son's age or younger or older?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was twice as old as my son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that's all I want to ask you about your relationship with him, but can you tell us what your son's relationship with Hamez Ukshini was in July of 1998, if you know? Don't speculate, but if you -- you can comment on what the nature and the state of that relationship was, please -- please tell us.

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that he knew him in that camp or whatever we can call him. I don't think they knew each other before they went -- my son went there as a soldiers -- as a soldier. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, for the purposes of the Prosecution, I don't need to carry the matter any further. I'm more than willing to assist the Trial Chamber if you wish me to explore the matter more deeply, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that we need to ask further questions for the witness. It seems that it would -- the notes would need -- the proofing note or the short message is not quite understandable anymore in -- let's -- let's put it directly, perhaps, to the witness. Are you aware of any problems your son may have had with Hamez Ukshini.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't know each other, Your Honour, they never had -- they could never have any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because this Chamber has received some information -- has received your earlier statement, but the Chamber has also received a very short note about a conversation you had with Mr. Di Fazio, and one line of this note reads as follows: "During this conversation, I informed Mr. Di Fazio that Hamez Ukshini was the enemy of my son." So it was reported to the Chamber that that is what you've told Mr. Di Fazio. Is that a mistake or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not a mistake; it is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then please explain to us, whereas you said that they didn't know each other, that nevertheless Ukshini was the enemy of your son.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or is it that you expressed your views on the events that have happened, and that that makes Ukshini an enemy. Is that how we have to understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For cross-examination, who will be the first one to cross-examine Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: With Your Honour's permission, Mr. Troop will cross-examine this witness first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Troop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'm grateful to the other Defence counsel for allowing me to go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Troop, who is counsel for Mr. Brahimaj. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I am counsel for Mr. Brahimaj, who sits behind me. I'd like to ask you some questions about events that took place in July 1998, specifically the time that you, your son, and Mahir Dema decided to join the Kosovo Liberation Army, the KLA.

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mahir Dema came to my house in Peje because he knew my son. Mahir had told my son that they had finished the house in Burimi Mountain and that they wanted to take some food to them. Then he told my son that he had been left alone, his friends had deserted him, so he came to fetch my son to go together. My son said, No, I can't go without asking my father's permission. And then we talked. And that Mahir begged me to let my son to go with him because he said, All the others have joined. And then I said, Okay, go, but take care until you go to Jabllanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. I'd like to ask you something -- I'd like now to ask you something about something that Mahir Dema said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Troop, it usually goes better if you just put a question to the witness because if you announce a certain line of questioning, then the witness picking up the subject starts talking, and it might be more efficient if you just put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. Madam Registrar, could we bring up document 3D010056?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has that received a number already, Mr. Troop?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, could you please assign a number to it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number D89, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Can we turn to the second page of that document, and perhaps we can bring up paragraph 2, please. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, what's the date of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: This is the statement of Mahir Dema -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: -- dated the 23rd of April, 2007. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you something that Mahir Dema has said to the Prosecution, Mr. Krasniqi. He says: "I do not remember the time or day or date when I decided to join the KLA. It was in 1998. Pal Krasniqi told me he knew the way, either because he had been to the KLA zone two weeks earlier or because he had stayed there for two weeks. I'm not sure what he told me." Mr. Krasniqi, you didn't know the way to Jablanica, did you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do because I am from that area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to speak closer to the microphone, when you are answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, could you please come closer to the microphone when answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, were you aware whether your son had been to the KLA in Jablanica before he left on the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard this, and I don't think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: The next time you heard from your son was the following day at 6.00 on the 11th of July. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th, not on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: He called you the following morning. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And he said that he'd been stopped at a check-point at Krusha e Madhe?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: He told you that he'd been beaten by the police at that check-point with his friend Mahir Dema?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: He also told you that he was taken to the police station in Klina, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And that he had been beaten further by the police at the police station?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Both he and Mahir Dema had been seriously beaten, according to what he told you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And he called you specifically to ask for your help, because he needed your help, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Now, it was -- you told him that you couldn't help him, could you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And the reason that you couldn't come to help was because the police were looking for you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Can you explain why the police were looking for you at that time?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was in prison, and Milutin Prascevic and the brothers and the sons of the person I killed in 1982 were looking for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about that in some more detail a little bit later, but I'd like to continue on the present topic. You --

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, can I ask you to bring up document U007 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Troop, I have first a question. Are you intending to tender it, the document you just read from?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: No, not at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be good if you indicate if you bring up a document just for reference or to read from, that there might be no need to give it a number. Madam Registrar, I don't know whether it can be unnumbered, but we are at such an early stage, I think we can reserve that number for other purposes. Now, the next document you would like to have on the screen, is that a document you would like to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Not at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at this stage. Then we do not -- if you then clearly quote from it - I don't know what kind of a document it is but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: It's the witness statement given to the Prosecution by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By this witness, yes. You just read then out the relevant portions, if at least you want to put them to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar, the document is U0079712.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's the 29th of February, 2004 statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And can we turn to page 3 of that document and bring up paragraph 13? I think it's the next page on the Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'd just like to read to you from a statement you gave to the Prosecution. And you told the Prosecution: "After the war had ended I searched for my son, I had met with Mahir twice ...?" Can you just confirm that it was two separate times that you met Mahir Dema?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him, but I wasn't looking for him and we met in Peje. And he said that until Kosovo is well liberated, I do not dare speak on the subject. So I have never met him since.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: How many times did you meet him, once or twice?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him once, and then I sent my wife and my nephew to Mahir Dema's house. But I haven't written this down on my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And Mahir Dema told you some things related to your son.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Can we bring up paragraph 9 of the statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And you said to the Prosecution that Mahir Dema had told you that: "When they reached Jablanica, Mahir was taken to hospital to be treated because he had been severely beaten, while my son had received a uniform ..." Is that what Mahir Dema told you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And then in the next paragraph, paragraph 10 of your statement, you say that Mahir Dema said that: "... after about a week at Jablanica, my son visited the hospital to see Mahir ..." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And you also told the Prosecution that Pal had gone to the hospital accompanied by two other soldiers. Is that what Mahir told you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about your meeting with Alush Agushi, and you knew Alush Agushi because he was the KLA commander at Jablanica, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And you met him at the police station in Klina?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And you explained yesterday what Alush Agushi told you, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And you remember saying that Alush Agushi had said to you that your son had been a soldier with him until the first offensive in September. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Would I be correct in thinking that you would not know personally when the offensives were around Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because I was in Peje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Could I -- if I could explain that the first offensive was actually around Jablanica at the start of August 1998, and the second offensive around Jablanica was towards the end of August and the start of September 1998, and then I'll ask you a question about that. But if that's correct, it doesn't make sense to talk about the first offensive as being in September, because, in fact, the first offensive was in August, early August; wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I heard. I, myself, didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: So it could be a mistake, either by yourself or by Alush Agushi as to which of the two offensives he was talking about? MR. DI FAZIO: I don't mind the question. I'm not objecting. I don't want to stand in the way of my colleague getting to his point, but it seems to me that it should be made clear that it's been put to the witness that he's mistaken when he reports to us through his statement that September was mentioned. So, in other words, it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think -- I think there are two options. Either the month is wrong -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or the sequence of offensives are wrong, and this all based on the assumption that there had been more offensives earlier than September. This comes down to logic on the basis of assumptions. I'm not excluding for the possibility that the witness could help us, but I would not too easily expect him to be able to do so. But, of course, you can put it to the witness. Mr. Krasniqi, one of the issues that comes up is that where you told us, or told the Prosecution and us, that your son stayed with Alush Agushi until the first offensive in September, that Mr. Troop expresses some doubt on whether that in September it was the first offensive or whether, perhaps, it was not September but another moment when the first offensive took place. Let's focus specifically on what Mr. Agushi told you. Did he use -- or did he mention September as the moment until when your son was with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that it wasn't my son who told me, but it was Alush Agushi who told me that up until the end of September he was with us and that he is somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any chance that you -- your recollection that he also told you that it was until the first offensive, that your recollection is not perfect in that respect, that he could have said offensive or not have said first offensive? How sure are you about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We knew that when the offensive started, they went -- attacked Jablanica and all the people went to the church of Gllogjan, and it was the first offensive and also Alush told me about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Troop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: You also said that Alush Agushi said that during the offensive, they were surrounded by the Serbs and had to retreat. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And that he told his soldiers to go in whichever direction they could to seek safety?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Subsequently, you reported the disappearance to the UNMIK office on missing persons and forensics, OMPF, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you bring up 65 ter document identification 928?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to tender it, Mr. Troop?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if no number has yet been assigned, a number should be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be then Exhibit Number D89, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Can we bring up page 3 of that document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm afraid this document has not been translated, so I will read relevant sections to you, and it will be translated for you. But you can see the document in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Troop, the -- at least the -- I have to move on to page 3 that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Your Honour, the initial page is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see the initial page is in more languages but not page 3. Yes. If you slowly read the relevant portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, this appears to be a victim identification form for your son Pal Krasniqi, and I think you can probably see his name at the top of the page, "Krasniqi, Pal." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I cannot see it because I can't see very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Perhaps we can enlarge the top half for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Some zooming-in would certainly assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Can we move to the bottom half of that document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: At the bottom of that document, there appears to be a signature of a person from the OMPF, and it's dated the 3rd of December, 2001. Can you see that in the bottom right-hand -- bottom right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the "12th of 01."

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I think it says, actually, the 3rd of the 12th/01.

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd of the 12th/01.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: You remember reporting the disappearance of your son to the OMPF, do you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which place has it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness speak to microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember where it is and where I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: It's not clear from this document, but it may be that it was in Peje.

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's the Red Cross, the International Red Cross in Krusha e Madhe, they came and we made a statement in our house to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Krasniqi, making a statement to someone around this time, the 3rd of December, 2001?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but it was a statement to the International Red Cross. There were two males and three females, and it was in Krusha e Madhe that I made this statement to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'd like to ask you some -- some questions which I will read in English, and they will be translated to you from this document. Point 4 of this document, it says: "Village/place where MP," missing person, "last seen." And next to that, it reads: "Nepolje" -- MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'm not objecting, I just want to be clear so I'm following the evidence. What we see before us, is that the statement made on the 3rd of December? Is that what counsel refers to? This is the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: This is a document recording the fact of a -- MR. DI FAZIO: I don't quarrel with that, but I just want to make sure that what we're looking at is a statement is what my learned friend Mr. Troop called the statement, it's this, it's not some other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Sorry, if there's any confusion, I'm referring to the document currently on the screen. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you very much. I'm grateful for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, can you remember the question or would you like me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading it, but I can't understand what's going on. I've forgotten things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Let me read it again to refresh your memory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Troop, because you had not put a question to the witness. You started reading but it's a bit difficult for the witness to remember a question which has not been put yet. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, this document says that the village/place where Pal Krasniqi was last seen was near Nepole. Do you remember telling anyone that that was where your son had last been seen?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but I said that they went together with friends to Nepole to buy cigarettes and food. There were five of them, and it was his friends who told me that they had seen my son buying things and that he went to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Why is it recorded here, presumably information from you, that your son was last seen in Nepole?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I've said that, but people said that he was seen in Nepole and that he disappeared soon after that. Some said that he went to Gllogjan and that he never returned. There are many rumours going around, but I didn't trust them because I wasn't on site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: The next section of this form says that your son Pal was last seen in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Troop, in order to avoid whatever confusion, first of all, of course, the questions on this form, which seems not to bear the signature of the witness, at least from what I have to assume - but you have not explored that - the signature at the bottom seems to be the rather of the officer who took the information. I would not even call it a statement. But the question, of course, is last when was the missing person last seen, could be a question when did you see the person for the last time or when, as far as you know, he was seen by whomever. So therefore, please keep that clearly in mind because the witness from his previous answer, I took it that there might be some confusion there which preferably should be avoided. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, the OMPF have recorded, presumably from you, that your son was last seen by somebody in September 1998. Now, did that information come from you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think I have said that because I didn't know that piece of information. I know now what I'm saying. In Jablanica, my -- my brother went to Jablanica together with members of the village to ask for my son, and then he -- they told them that he either went towards Peje or Klina. But I haven't made that statement. That piece of information may have been given by somebody else, but not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'll move on, Mr. Krasniqi. Mr. Krasniqi, I understand you have a sister called Marijana. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she is not my sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: How is Marijana related to you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm hearing it for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Can I ask you, Mr. Krasniqi, whether you know an individual called Dede Deda?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: As I understand it - and I may be mistaken - he is your nephew. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: He is the son of your sister?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And he and your son were, despite being slightly different ages, were good friends?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And they met around twice a week until the conflict or the fighting broke out?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my son went to his place and he came to our place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: They knew each other very well, did they not?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because they are relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, can I ask that you bring up document 3D01-0017?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any intention to tender it, Mr. Troop?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then a number should be assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number D90, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm going to ask you to look at a statement given by Dede Deda, your nephew?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: This is a document which has only been provided in English; we do not have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'd like you to -- I'd like to read to you from the paragraphs and ask you questions based on those paragraphs, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Can we bring up paragraph 4, please, on the second page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Dede Deda says this about your son: "Being asked about the person of Pal Krasniqi and I can state as follows: Pal was the son of my uncle from my mother's side. Although he was a few years younger than me, we had a very good relation. Besides the fact" --

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: -- "that we were blood-related, I considered him also as a very good friend and we did a lot of things together."

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: "We met each other approximately twice a week until the conflict broke out."

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Now, that information is true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'd like to read out another paragraph and ask you whether or not you were aware of this information, so please wait for the question, but I'll read the paragraph out slowly first. Dede Deda says this: "The last personal contact I had with him was in the middle of August 1998. It was around the Catholic holiday, which is celebrated on the 15th of August. Pal called me at home and told me that he is in Jablanica. He informed me that he had a lot of money with him and therefore wanted to meet with me in Gjakove. As a meeting point we agreed on a place where we used to play pool together. The meeting was set up for the same day. Pal didn't say more during this telephone conversation." Then the next paragraph: "After I had received the call, I went the designated place; however, Pal didn't show up as agreed. At this point in time, there was no way to get in contact with him and therefore I went back home. I never heard from him again and I was still hoping that he would be alive somewhere." Now, the question is this: Did Dede Deda tell you about the conversation that he'd had with your son around the middle of August?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'd like to come back, Mr. Krasniqi, to something you mentioned much earlier on in the evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, I note the time is half past 10.00. Perhaps this might be a convenient break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If this is a convenient moment for you, then we'll have a break and in view of the redactions to be made, the break should be half an hour. We'll then resume at 11.00. But could you give us an indication how much more time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I would estimate about 15 to 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And other counsel would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very little, if any time at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because, of course, I am thinking about the next witness as well, who is scheduled for one hour. Would there be a possibility that the parties agree during the next break to what extent and what portions the Prosecution could lead because that saves a lot of time. If that's not possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can indicate now that I'm not going to be in a position to agree to the leading of any evidence from that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, moreover, that the cross-examination of that witness on my behalf will not be short, unless Your Honour imposes a time-limit on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I'm seeking is to get through the evidence with utmost precision but then as quick as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Troop, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'm going to ask you some further questions just for a short period. The first thing I'd like to ask you about is something that you said just before the break. And you said: "My brother went to Jablanica together with members of the village to ask for my son, and they told him that he either went towards Peje or Klina." Now, which brother is this? What's your brother's name?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He died on New Year's night. His name was Hil.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'm sorry to hear that, Mr. Krasniqi. Do you remember when he went to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they shelled, when the Serb forces shelled our village, all of the people moved out of the villages to Jablanica to the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wherever they could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Do you remember the year, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Sunday, the 2nd of July, when they attacked our village and they burned it to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Was that in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'd just like to clarify this, Mr. Krasniqi, because you have said that your son left on the 10th of July, 1998, but that your brother went to ask for Pal at some point. Logically, that must have been after the 10th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was after that because I heard that he went to -- they went to Jablanica and they couldn't meet him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And he told you that Pal had either gone towards Peje or Klina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, you have misunderstood that. When they asked for him, they were told, We will ask because we saw them in -- Pal Krasniqi in Jablanica. They went to the villages of Zhabel and Grgoc, and several soldiers were told that -- my brother was 56 at the time, and they were told that he had been taken to Peje. But we Albanians know what it means, the expression: "Go to Peje."

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'd like to move back in time, Mr. Krasniqi, to something that happened in the early 1980s --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Troop, it would be a good idea that the Chamber also gets to know what Albanians understand by: "Go to Peje."

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I was always taught in advocacy never to ask a question where I don't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is sometimes different --

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Would you like to ask the question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you insist. Mr. Krasniqi, what do Albanians think the expression "Go to Peje" means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour, to say that it's a banal word, expression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vulgar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll not be shocked by it, especially the way you introduced it makes clear that you're aware that the language is not specifically yours. Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be interpreted in two ways. When -- when they were told, Your cousin has either been taken to Peje or to Klina, and the expression goes: "Go to Peje, sod off." These are the two meanings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's still not entirely clear, Mr. -- just use the words you would use in your village. Tell us what it means: "Go to Peje."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's the literal sense of the expression, but the way it was used when it was used in the context, it was -- it was said to mean that your godfather has disappeared, not to return ever again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So just -- do I understand that this means he went to a place from where he'll never return? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, and I know that there may be a linguistic issue here, but page 38, line 14, does Your Honour see the words: "Go to Peje, sod off"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't know whether the expression "sod off" is familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not familiar. If you have some language that could explain it to us --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, it's an expletive. It, I think -- I don't know how much of an explanation you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Is it "get lost" or "go to hell"?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Stronger language than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In stronger language than that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then at least it has been clarified, so now not only Albanians but also others do understand. Please proceed, Mr. Troop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: So your brother -- was it your brother who was told to get lost, in colloquial terms?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother and his several friends were told that my son had been sent either to Peje or to Klina. That means getting a one-way ticket; that is, going on a one-way journey, not to return again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I'd like to bring you to events of the early 1980s and something -- as I understand that your neighbour at the time was a person called Miodrag Saric. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And at sometime in 1982, he injured your brother Prenk [phoen] with an axe. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: There was a -- there was a dispute between the two of you, and it was something to do with animals grazing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Was -- what ethnicity was Miodrag Saric? Was he a Serb or a Montenegrin?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And of what ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: His mother was Montenegrin, and he was from Bosnia-Herzegovina, he'd come from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And the result of the -- as a result of the dispute, you took a gun and shot him, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but, sir, have you called me here to talk about this or what? I'm sorry to have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Krasniqi, but I just need to explain and have the Court understand why the Serbs were looking for you so many years later, and I think this puts it into context, just for your information. And you were convicted, weren't you, by a court and sentenced to 15 years imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And I'm sure you remember at the time, it was widely reported in the media, in the newspapers, on the radio --

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: You may not know it, but it was also reported in international press. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the media wrote about it, the radio had the story. Although I killed him, but I was sentenced and convicted without the respect of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I understand that. You served close to the full sentence of 15 years, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 12 years and a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And again, when you were released, even after you were released, the fact that you had killed Miodrag Saric was reported again in the media, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And it was widely known what had happened so many years before?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Can you explain who Milutin Prascevic is, please?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew his father and his grandfather. He was a commander for the area, including Gjakove, that was for killing people -- for ordering the killing of Albanians and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: What was his -- what was his position? You said he was commander, but he was commander of what?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of the Gjakove area for all the territory of the Gjakove region.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Was he a police commander?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of all of the police, of the army. Nobody dared to oppose him, to challenge him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And you said that the brothers and the sons of Miodrag Saric were also looking for you in 1998. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: They must have been looking for you for some time?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were looking for me in Klina, and I had left Klina and moved to Peje. And they ordered the Klina police to capture me, and they called Peje but they didn't know me in Peje. That's how I escaped. I was staying -- I was staying in Peje without an address, a publicly known address.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: How long had you been having problems with the police in the area?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998, there were killings and -- but up until 1999, everybody had left Peje but I stayed there. And then I went to the train station and moved out of Peje in the opposite direction to reach Klina and the village of Krusheva. And that's where I stayed with my wife's relatives until the war was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Not only the police, but also the brothers and the sons of Miodrag Saric were looking for you to take revenge, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: All the police knew who you were, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everybody knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And when Pal was detained in the police station on the 10th and 11th -- on the police station on the 10th and 11th of July, 1998, they would have known that he was your son, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And no doubt your son had had problems, simply by virtue of the fact that he was the son of someone who had killed a Serb, Miodrag Saric?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: A Serb, or whatever his ethnicity was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Judge Hoepfel, for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from that, if there would be a possibility to lay a foundation on what in the police station on the 10th and 11th of July, what would have been known, that's of course -- I don't know to what extent the witness can give any factual foundation for what at first sight looks more an inference or perhaps even speculation. Please, if you could do that, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: You spoke to Pal Krasniqi on the early morning of either the 10th or the 11th of July, 1998, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And he said that he had been detained by the Serbian police in Klina police station, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And he told you that he'd been interrogated and asked who he was, where he was going?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't say that, but I was told about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: It would have been --

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rather, he told me -- he asked me to help him get out of there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And did the -- did he tell you whether the police knew who he was, that he was your son?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he knew him, the police knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And when you say the police knew him, you mean to say that the police knew that he was your son?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Just wait there, for a second, whilst I confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. Those are the questions I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to have one matter clarified in relation to these last questions. Could you tell us, Mr. Krasniqi, you said the police knew who your son was and that he was your son. In this telephone conversation or in your conversations later with Mahir, did they tell you in more detail what the police knew about your son and his father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When -- my son went to the elementary school in Klina, and the disagreements -- due to the disagreements between Albanians and Serbs at school, he was quarrelling with them. He had rows with the Serbs, and they knew that I was in prison at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did your son tell you specifically that reference was made by the police when on the 10th or the 11th of July, specifically reference was made to -- well, that's to say your past, that is, the fact that you had been convicted for killing Mr. Saric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't hear any such thing, and I didn't meet my son after that to hear what he was actually told when he was being beaten up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I say, therefore, that it was your assumption that they would have been known, is that correct, or is there any further information that makes you believe that those police officers were aware of your past?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they knew my son. They knew that he was my son, and they knew me, the police, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then again, is that just your assumption or who did tell you exactly what the police asked or said at that moment, the 10th and the 11th of July, which further supports your belief that they were aware of your past?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were several incidents with the police when I was released from prison. The young people at school, they divided in two camps: The Serbian boys on one side and the Albanians on the other, and they fought against each other. And that's why I thought that they knew who he was, and before he left I advised him, Take care of yourself because you're young.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And may I just get back to that one sentence when you said to your son when he got out of, to take care. You first mentioned a while ago you connected this somehow with the place he was going to. Did I misunderstand you or did you specifically warn him to take care when going to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, when he was in Klina -- because when he went to Jablanica, then I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Just before when he left, I mean, did you give him a special warning or what was the gist of what you said to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I advised him when he left, when he set out together with Mahir to go to Jablanica, I told him to avoid check-points, which were very many at the time, because the police will recognise you and they may kill you and you're young. So when you go there, try to go via Bistrica to Jablanica, but unfortunately they were held at a check-point and that's where they were stuck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Troop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's just one point which I suggest might assist with clarifying, and that's how the witness knew the information about what had happened at the police station on the 10th, 11th July. Perhaps I could ask one or two questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would like to, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, we know that your son was detained in the Klina police station on the 10th or 11th of July and that he told you that by telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Did you speak to Mahir Dema later about what had happened in the police station with Pal Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when he was released, it was after the war, because in the meantime I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And when you spoke to Mahir Dema about what had happened that night, did he tell you what had happened to both of them -- both of them in the police station?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: And that's the basis for your understanding that the police recognised him and knew who he was?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police knew from before who he was, but when they took them to Klina at night and when they read their driving licence, they beat Mahir Dema more, they asked -- telling him: Why have you come here to Klina from Istog and because he was a Muslim, because they used these religious differences, you know, to -- against them. There was a Serb there, a high-ranking leader in Kline, he recognised my son because those from Belgrade, of course, didn't know who Pal was, and they beat them, but they beat Mahir more than my son because this person who knew my son said, Don't beat him so much because he's a good lad. That's why they refrained from beating him as much as they did Mahir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless then, two follow-up questions in this respect, Mr. Krasniqi. You said it was a Serb, a high-ranking leader, in Klina. Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lazar Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, who told you that this man had said, Don't beat him so much because he's a good lad? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mahir told me. He said it was a policeman who saved Pal because those were about to kill us. They told my son to go home and they wanted to keep Mahir, but my son said, I won't leave this place alone without Mahir because they left together, intending to go where they wanted, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then they were held up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, Mr. Guy-Smith, any need for further questions in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, any need to re-examine the witness? MR. DI FAZIO: Just one or two very brief matters, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. Re-examination by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you were asked some questions about -- arising from a statement that Dede Deda gave, and I'd like you to just look at some of those aspects of that statement. MR. DI FAZIO: So could that statement, please, be made available on the screen; it's D90, I believe. Okay. It's the second page that I'm interested in, page 2 of 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: You were asked in cross-examination by counsel for the Defence did -- this question: "Did Dede Deda tell you about the conversation he had with your son around the middle of August?" And you said: "Yes." And you were shown the statement and it -- when did you speak to Dede Deda and when did he report to you this conversation that he had had with your son Pal in the middle of August 1998? When did you speak to Deda -- Dede, rather?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke after I made the statements, because he was reluctant to tell me then. Hearing words here and there, he told me what happened. He told me, You know that we were together, and I feel sorry that no sign is seen of him anywhere. And then he explained to me what they had talked between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: When Dede Deda reported this to you, did he provide any details as to where Pal apparently was when he made the phone call?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in Jablanica and with his mobile phone or walkie-talkie they talked, and he explained that he was in Jabllanice, telling him that I have a lot of money and that you should wait for me at this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Okay. And they were the details that Dede Deda told you; correct? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Did your son own a mobile phone?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had a mobile phone or his friends had, but Dede told me that they had spoken on the phone. And I said, This is a secret, beware, you shouldn't talk, you know, civilians and army members.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber if at the time in -- and I'm talking about August 1998, there were any telephone connections with Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have fixed-line, but whoever could afford it bought mobile phones and those which are called walkie-talkie. I don't know where they found them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Did your son have a lot of money with him when he left you on July 10?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, he didn't. Maybe he had 50 Deutschemarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: What work was your son doing at the time? What was his job?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He just helped out someone doing errands here and there, physical, manual labour, and we were paid for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Did Ded -- I'm sorry, I'll get this name right eventually. Did Dede Deda comment or provide you with any information as to the manner of speech, the way Pal Krasniqi spoke when he made contact with this mobile phone or walkie-talkie?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was a brief conversation, at least this is what he told me; it didn't last long. Of course, they were afraid lest someone might intercept their conversation, that's why they didn't speak at length.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: When you say: "They were afraid lest someone might intercept their conversation," is that something you think was a consideration that they were taking into account, or you were told that that was the reason why they didn't talk long?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Dede talked with my son, they kept it brief. This is what he told me. And then he went out to wait for my son, who never showed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions, I take it, from Defence counsel? Mr. Krasniqi, this concludes your evidence in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague and for having answered all the questions. If you would excuse me for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I, therefore, wish you a safe trip home again. Before I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom, I'd like to hear from the parties whether the usher on his way back could immediately bring the next witness. Mr. Re, next witness could be brought into the courtroom right away?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. No protective measures are required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Usher, would you escort Mr. Krasniqi out of the courtroom. I wish you a safe trip home, again, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at the clock, I see that we have got another two hours, of which 20 minutes will be taken by a break, that means 1 hour and 40 minutes. The parties are encouraged to use that time as efficiently as possible, so in order to see whether it would be possible to finish the witness today so that he can return, especially because we're not sitting next Monday. He would have to stay for quite a while in The Hague perhaps just for 15 or 20 minutes. So the parties are encouraged to see what they can do in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is there any possibility, Your Honour, in the next break of ascertaining whether there's any room for flexibility in terms of continuing on, a little beyond quarter to 2.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course we'll do that. At the same time, it's not only courtroom time, it's also what we can ask from interpreters and transcribers.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I understand. I entirely understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is limited. So I would very much encourage the parties to see whether they could even conclude with the witness without an additional request. Meanwhile, I take the time to say a few words about scheduling. On the 6th of June, I think that was already announced, we are not sitting because the Appeals Chamber needs the courtroom. Earlier, I've announced that we would try to swap the 15th of June, that is a Friday, usually we are not sitting on a Friday, from afternoon to morning; that turns out to be impossible. That means in that week, Monday, the 11th, we are not sitting. We are sitting on the 12th, the 13th, and the 14th, and on that Friday, the 15th of June, we'll sit in the afternoon and not in the morning. Then as far as the other Fridays are concerned in the month of June, that is the 8th, we are not sitting; the 22nd we're not sitting; and on the Friday, the 29th, we are not sitting either.
